standard.title: European Imperial Expansion and Movement of Peoples
standard.description: the causes and effects of European imperial expansion and the movement of peoples in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, and the different responses to colonisation and migration
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can describe the features of societies and the effects of contact and change in earlier periods (AC9HH8K07, AC9HH8K08, AC9HH8K12). They have not yet examined the global scale of European imperial expansion in the modern period, the push and pull factors driving mass population movements, or the range of responses by colonised peoples to European contact.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify and describe the causes of European imperial expansion and the movement of peoples — including push and pull factors — describe the effects of those movements on colonised peoples, and describe the different responses to colonisation and migration across affected societies.

nodes.label: European imperial expansion — scale and drivers
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the scale of European imperial expansion in the late 18th and early 19th centuries and identify the main drivers — economic, political, technological and ideological — that enabled and motivated it.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe European expansion as a global phenomenon, name at least two regions affected (e.g. Australia, India, Africa, Americas), and identify at least two drivers of expansion.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the geographic scope of British, French, Spanish and Portuguese expansion; explain the economic motivations (raw materials, markets, trade routes); the political competition between European powers; the role of Industrial Revolution technology in enabling long-distance settlement and control; the ideological justifications (civilising mission, racial hierarchy); connect to the prior Y8 empires content.
wider: Compare the motivations and methods of British expansion with those of another European imperial power (e.g. France in North Africa, the Dutch in the East Indies) — identifying what was shared and what was distinctive
Examine how European powers justified imperial expansion through racial and civilisational ideology — and how those justifications were contested by colonised peoples
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding imperial expansion as a driven, structured phenomenon — not random — is the prerequisite for understanding the movement of peoples node (N2). Students who cannot explain why European powers expanded cannot explain the push and pull mechanisms that drove population movements, and cannot evaluate responses to colonisation meaningfully.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat imperial expansion as self-explanatory ('Europeans wanted power') without understanding the specific economic, technological and ideological mechanisms. Making these explicit as a causal framework is the scaffold for analysing population movements and colonisation responses.

success_criteria: Describes the geographic scale of European imperial expansion with at least two regional examples
Identifies at least two drivers of imperial expansion and explains how each contributed

nodes.label: Push and pull factors — causes of population movement
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the push factors that drove people to leave their homelands and the pull factors that attracted them to new destinations, across voluntary and forced migration.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify at least two push factors (e.g. Agricultural Revolution disruption, famine, persecution, forced removal) and two pull factors (e.g. land, employment, freedom) and describe each with an example.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the full range of push factors — Agricultural Revolution enclosures, Industrial Revolution displacement, Irish Potato Famine, religious and political persecution, forced migration via slavery and convict transportation; and pull factors — land availability, employment, escape from rigid class structures, personal freedom; distinguish voluntary from forced migration; use data on movement scales (numbers transported, nations involved) to ground the analysis; connect push/pull to the imperial expansion drivers from N1.
wider: Examine data on the transatlantic slave trade — the scale, routes, nations involved — and evaluate what the data reveals about the nature of forced migration as distinct from voluntary movement

Compare the push-pull framework for two different migrations (e.g. Irish famine migration vs convict transportation) — identifying what the framework explains well and where it breaks down for forced migration

response_modes.reason: Students commonly conflate voluntary and forced migration within the push-pull framework, treating slavery and convict transportation as though individuals were responding to incentives. Making the distinction between coercive and voluntary movement explicit is conceptually important and prevents misapplication of the framework.

success_criteria: Identifies and describes at least two push factors and two pull factors with examples
Distinguishes voluntary migration from forced migration and explains how the push-pull framework applies differently to each

nodes.label: Effects on colonised peoples
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the effects of European expansion and population movement on colonised peoples — including dispossession, disease, destruction of traditional society and culture — and explain how these effects operated.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least three distinct effects of colonisation on colonised peoples (e.g. dispossession of land, introduced disease, disruption of cultural practices) and explain how each operated.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain the mechanisms of dispossession (legal fictions, military force, treaty exploitation); the catastrophic effect of introduced diseases on populations with no prior immunity; the systematic disruption of traditional governance, economy, religion and culture; the deliberate and incidental destruction of cultural knowledge and practice; examine specific examples from at least two regions (e.g. First Nations Australians, Indigenous peoples of the Americas, African societies).
wider: Compare the scale and nature of demographic collapse across different colonised populations — examining what the data reveals about the relative weight of disease vs direct violence vs social disruption as causes of population decline
Examine how colonised peoples experienced and described the effects of European contact in their own terms — using sources from colonised peoples rather than colonisers' accounts

response_modes.reason: Students commonly reduce colonisation effects to 'bad things happened' without understanding the distinct mechanisms — disease, dispossession, cultural destruction — and how each operated differently across contexts. Multiple regional examples build the fuller picture the descriptor requires.

success_criteria: Describes at least three distinct effects of colonisation on colonised peoples
Explains the mechanisms by which at least two effects operated

nodes.label: Different responses to colonisation and migration
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the different responses of colonised and migrant peoples to European expansion and movement — including resistance, accommodation, adaptation, and contribution — and explain what shaped each response.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least two distinct types of response (e.g. armed resistance, accommodation, cultural adaptation) and give one example of each from the period.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the range of responses — armed resistance (frontier wars, slave rebellions), diplomatic negotiation, accommodation and adoption of settler practices, contribution to colonial economies and industries on colonised peoples' own terms, formation of new cultural identities; explain what factors shaped which response was available or chosen; use examples from multiple contexts (First Nations Australians, enslaved Africans, Irish migrants, convicts); connect the diversity of responses to the diversity of circumstances.
wider: Examine a specific resistance movement or leader (e.g. Pemulwuy, Toussaint Louverture) in depth — analysing what strategies were used, what the response achieved, and what it reveals about the possibilities and limits of resistance

Compare how responses to colonisation differed between groups with different levels of political organisation, population size, or geographic position — identifying structural factors that shaped what was possible
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Resistance movement case studies offer genuine depth — students can analyse agency, strategy, and outcome rather than treating colonised peoples as passive recipients of European expansion. This is also a strong source analysis opportunity using accounts from colonised peoples themselves.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly frame responses as either resistance or submission without recognising the full range — adaptation, contribution, cultural synthesis, negotiation — that characterises actual responses across different groups and contexts.

success_criteria: Describes at least two distinct types of response to colonisation with examples from the period
Explains what factors shaped which responses were available or chosen in a given context
